title: Generative AI Act II: Test Time Scaling Drives Cognition Engineering
extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and technical position paper about a new paradigm the authors call “cognition engineering.” It argues that first-generation large language models mainly excel at knowledge retrieval and prompt-based interaction, but remain limited by shallow reasoning, knowledge latency, and weak deliberation. The paper’s central question is how generative AI can move beyond static knowledge generation toward deeper, more human-like cognitive processes.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any participant population. Instead, it synthesizes prior work on test-time scaling and related training strategies, including parallel sampling, tree search, multi-turn correction, long chain-of-thought reasoning, reinforcement learning, and self-training. It frames these methods as mechanisms for allocating more computation at inference time and for shaping models to reason more deliberately.

The authors position cognition engineering as a systematic methodology for constructing AI systems that can think, reason, and problem-solve more deeply. They conclude that test-time scaling is the most immediate practical bridge from current LLMs to this new paradigm, and they outline a roadmap for applying these methods across domains. The paper is theoretical and tutorial-oriented rather than empirical, and it does not involve K-12 learners, teachers, or classrooms.

identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a conceptual/theoretical overview of cognition engineering and test-time scaling in generative AI; it does not evaluate a specific product in a K-12 reading or literacy intervention.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/framework paper about cognition engineering and test-time scaling, not an empirical study with student outcomes or a controlled design. No K-12 intervention, comparator, or measurable literacy outcome is reported.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational impact is measured or demonstrated in the paper. The text discusses potential applications of generative AI broadly, but provides no effect on reading, literacy, or student performance.
